title: 逮捕状の「電子令状」4都県から
body:
逮捕状などをオンラインで請求・発付する「電子令状」について、最高裁は裁判所での導入スケジュールを決めた。まずは覚醒剤所持・使用事件を対象として、今年度中に東京など首都圏１都３県の裁判所で運用を始める。来年５月に大阪や福岡などでもスタートさせ、７月には全国で全事件を取り扱う。土日などの対応は東京と大阪の裁判所に集約する。【一覧表】電子令状の「導入スケジュール」
刑事手続きをＩＴ化する改正刑事訴訟法が、来年３月までに施行されるのに合わせた措置。大幅な運用変更となることから、最高裁は各裁判所での状況を検証しながら、対象とする地域や事件を広げていく考えだ。裁判の証拠などもＩＴ化され、捜査の迅速化や現場の負担軽減が期待される。
逮捕状や捜索令状は現在、警察官らが各裁判所に出向いて請求書と関係資料を提出し、裁判官が内容を審査して紙で発付している。改正刑訴法により、電子データに旧来の紙と同じ効力が認められる。警察官らは裁判所へ行かずに端末上で関係資料を添えて電子令状を請求し、発付を受ける。執行時は電子令状をタブレットなどで示す。
最高裁が、１都３県の東京、神奈川、埼玉、千葉にある裁判所で電子令状の運用を始めるのは、人員体制が整っているためだ。覚醒剤の所持・使用事件は、違法な薬物成分が検出されたとする鑑定結果など証拠が定型的で、公判の争点も明確なケースが多く、安定的な導入が可能と判断した。
来年５月からは、１都３県で全事件を取り扱うほか、大阪や愛知、福岡、北海道など高裁のある７道府県でも覚醒剤所持・使用事件で対応を始める。７月には、全国で全事件の対応に踏み切る見通しだ。
運用にあたっては、弁護人ら事件関係者を除き外部からは接続できない新たな事件管理システムを導入する。警察や検察のシステムと連携する。
改正法の施行後、業務の合理化を図るため土日祝日や平日夜の令状審査は、東京、大阪の裁判所に集約する。主に東日本の事件は東京地裁、西日本の事件は大阪地裁で対応する方向だ。

title: フランス各地で暴動 2400人逮捕
body: Sybille de La Hamaide　Clotaire Achi　Abdul Saboor[パリ／リモージュ １８日 ロイター] - フランスのマクロン大統領は１８日、物価高や公共サービスの質低下に抗議す‌る前日のデモが国内各地で暴動に発展したことを⁠受け、国民に冷静な対応を呼びかけた。暴動は同国で近年最悪規模となり、数千人が逮捕され、商​店が略奪や破壊の被害を受けた。マクロン氏はテレビ放映された国民向け演説で「こうした映像を‌見て、われわれは皆、彼らは何を考えていたのか、フランス人がどうしてフランスにこんなことをできるの‌かと自問した」と述べ‌た。「何をもってしても正当化も説明も​弁解もできない。今夜、われわれは皆、怒りと恥ずかしさを感‌じている」と語った。１７日の暴動は、マクロン氏に対する根深い怒りを浮き彫りにした。‌マクロン氏は２０２７年に退​任する予定だが、１０年に及ぶ在任期間は社会不満の‌高まり、経済の低迷、債務の膨張に特徴付けられるようになってい⁠る。マクロン氏は、平和的に抗議していた人々の不満には正当な理由があるとし、混乱を引き起こそうとする人々の行動と混同すべきではないと述⁠べた。一部の右派政治家が求めていた非常事​態宣言は見送った。‌ただ、公共施設や地元商店を守るために必要な場合、知事がデモを禁止できるよう政府として措置を講じるとした。ヌニェ⁠ス内相によると、１７日にはパリのデモで参加者１人が心停止⁠で死亡した。全国で２４００人が逮捕され、警官約１０００人が負傷した。パリのレピュ⁠ブリック広場では１８日午後、警察とデモ参加者が再び衝突し、警察が催涙ガス‌を使用し⁠た。デモ参加者は積み上げられた自転車に火を放った。​ロイターの記者によると、現場には数百人のデモ参加者がいたとみられる。

title: 横浜前市長 パワハラに厳しい審判
body:
１８日に投開票された横浜市長選は、自民、日本維新の会、国民民主の各党地元支部と公明党市議団の支援を受けた新人で弁護士の原沢敦美さん（５９）が初当選を果たした。市職員へのパワーハラスメント行為が認定された前市長の山中竹春さん（５４）は出直し選挙に臨んだが、厳しい審判を受けることになった。【写真】当選確実となり、万歳をして喜ぶ原沢氏（１８日午後８時１分）
「市民の厳しい受け止めが反映された結果だ」。原沢さんの当選確実が伝えられると、山中さんは取材に答え、パワハラ問題の影響をそう振り返った。
市の部長が山中さんのパワハラ問題を公表した１月以降、市政は揺れた。７月には第三者調査委員がパワハラ行為を認定。９月に市内で開かれた国際会議や来年３月に開幕する国際園芸博覧会（ＧＲＥＥＮ×ＥＸＰＯ）の半年前イベントは、市長不在で行われる事態となっていた。読売新聞が１８日に５６か所の投票所で実施した出口調査では、「大いに」と「ある程度」を含めて８割が投票にあたりパワハラ問題を「考慮した」と回答した。
自民は昨年の前回選で支援した山中さんと決別。過去の東京都大田区長選で名前が浮上した原沢さんに白羽の矢を立てた。維新、国民民主、公明から支援を取り付けて包囲網を敷き、経済界もバックアップした。
政党や経済界の多くの支援を失った山中さんの陣営では、ＩＲ（カジノを含む統合型リゾート）計画を巡り「再誘致の動きがある」とけん制し、再争点化を狙った。自民や地元経済界が進めたＩＲ誘致を巡っては、２０２１年の市長選で山中さんが撤回を掲げて初当選を果たした経緯があった。ただ、原沢さんを含め、他の候補はすべて誘致を否定。陣営関係者は「５年前のように市民が関心を持ってくれなかった」と話す。
原沢さんは「政治経験はないが、市民にとって何が一番大事かを第一に考え、横浜をいい街にしていきたい」と意気込みを語った。

title: サイバー攻撃 なぜ日本が狙われる
body:
日本の企業や自治体を狙ったサイバー攻撃が相次ぎ、個人情報の流出が後を絶たない。米紙ニューヨーク・タイムズも日本のセキュリティ対策の遅れを指摘している。しかし、なぜ日本がこれほど狙われるのか。背景には、攻撃技術の進歩だけでなく、盗み出した個人情報を詐欺に利用できるという犯罪組織側の事情がある。日本人の個人情報そのものが、攻撃者にとって魅力的な商品になっているのではないか。
米紙が報じる「日本がサイバー攻撃の格好の標的になる理由」出典：クーリエ・ジャポン　2026/10/18(日)
今、日本が一番狙われている　2025年全世界のメール脅威のうち、1月は69.5%、2月は80.2％が日本をターゲットに出典：Proofpoint　2025/3/23(日)
Proofpointの調査では、2025年1月に同社が観測した新種のメール攻撃の69.5％、2月には80.2％が日本を標的としていた。ただし、世界中のサイバー攻撃の8割が日本に向けられたという意味ではない。なぜ攻撃者が日本を選ぶのか。
国民性として、世界と比較して、詐欺の被害に遭う危機意識に乏しいということは否めない。盗まれた氏名、住所、電話番号、メールアドレスなどは、それ自体が犯罪者にとって価値を持つ。複数の情報を組み合わせれば、相手の勤務先や家族構成まで把握し、本人の事情を熟知した人物を装う詐欺にも利用できる。
攻撃側の技術も変わった。生成AIによって自然な日本語の詐欺メールを容易に作れるようになり、脆弱性の発見にもAIが使われ始めている。Microsoftが今年10月に修正した脆弱性は、同社製品全体で約1400件に達した。近年の年間修正件数に匹敵する規模である。
もっとも、修正件数の増加が攻撃の増加を直接示すわけではない。日本が狙われる理由を考える際には、盗んだ情報の使い道にも目を向けるべきだ。相次ぐ情報漏えいの背後には、特殊詐欺などで個人情報を悪用する犯罪市場の存在があると考えられる。

title: 東芝 難関大生から再評価される今
body: 2015年に発覚した不正会計問題などで経営危機に陥り、上場廃止となった「東芝」。ところがAI時代を迎え、難関大学の理系学生から改めて注目されている。なぜいま、東芝が選ばれているのか。【一覧】2026年度最新　主要国公立大学の「人気企業115社」就職者数はこちら＊　　＊　　＊かつて経営危機が報じられた「東芝」がいま、難関大生から再評価されている。就職支援サイト「ワンキャリア」に掲載されている口コミでは、東芝は「技術力を高められそう」「未来を創る安心・安全」「就職先としてかなり人気」と新卒学生から称賛されているのだ。東芝は2015年に不正会計が発覚し、23年に株式上場を廃止。経営の立て直しを進めるなかで26年度は東京大から8人が就職した。理系学生の人気企業ランキング（27年卒マイナビ・日経大学生就職企業人気ランキング）は、前年の89位から74位に上昇した。さらに夏季・冬季インターンシップの受け入れ人数は、ここ2年で倍増。23年度は約600人だったが、25年度は2倍の1200人を受け入れた。今年度はさらに増加見込みだという。とはいえ、不祥事のニュースを覚えている親から子どもが東芝に就職するのを心配されることはないのだろうか。「少なくとも私が担当する範囲では、親御さんから反対されたので説得するための材料がほしい、などの相談を内定者から受けたことはありません」と、採用センターの熊谷真由美さんは言う。■学生が説明会で「えっ」追い風の一つは、やはりAIだ。生成AIの普及により、データセンターのエネルギー需要に対応する送変電配電事業や、膨大なデータの保存を担うハードディスクドライブ（HDD）などの事業が好調だ。26年4～6月期の営業損益と売上高営業利益率（ROS）、当期純損益は過去最高、営業損益は前年同期比2.8倍の1119億円だった。だが、就活を始めたばかりの学生たちが抱く東芝のイメージは“今の姿”ではないという。熊谷さんは言う。「接点のある学生さんの半分くらいは、いまだに東芝を白物家電のメーカーだと思っています」いまも“東芝ブランド”の冷蔵庫や洗濯機は売られているが、家電事業はすでに中国の家電大手である美的集団に売却されている。「送変電配電、量子暗号通信などの事業を紹介すると、学生さんの反応が変わりますね。いま、東芝はBtoBの企業なのですと説明すると、『えっ』と驚くように顔を上げる学生さんもいます」（熊谷さん）

title: 米中間選挙 争点にデータセンター
body: 11月3日投開票の米中間選挙で、人工知能（AI）ブームに伴い全米各地で整備が進むデータセンターが重要な争点に浮上している。【写真】米中西部オハイオ州コロンバス近郊のデータセンター特にバンス副大統領のお膝元、中西部オハイオ州では与党共和党が牙城とする農村部を中心に計画が急増。環境破壊などへの懸念から反発が広がり、上院選や知事選で共和党が思わぬ苦戦を強いられている。敗北すればバンス氏にも痛手だ。◇党派超え団結「データセンターはいらない！」。州都コロンバスから車で約1時間半の町ピクア。中心部で今月6日、住民グループがプラカードを掲げ、データセンター整備への抗議活動を行った。近くを通る車から時折、応援のクラクションが響く。活動を率いる農家のアリーシャ・ラングさん（43）は「共和や民主、無党派の違いを超え、私たちは団結している」と語る。問題となっているのは、米IT大手メタ（旧フェイスブック）が東京ドーム52個分の広さに相当する約2．5平方キロの農地で計画するデータセンターだ。水の大量使用や水質汚染、電気料金高騰などへの不安が広がるほか、不透明な決定プロセスや税制優遇措置に対する不満も噴出している。オハイオは既にデータセンターの数が200超に上り、米国内で有数の集積地だ。さらにピクアのような農村部でIT大手の新規大型案件が相次ぎ、州南部ではソフトバンクグループも大規模施設を計画する。ピクアを含むマイアミ郡は共和党色が強い地域で、民主党のバイデン前大統領が勝利した2020年大統領選でも、トランプ大統領は7割を超える票を獲得した。ラングさんも共和党支持者として有権者登録をしている。ただ、地元の共和党議員がデータセンターに関する相談に全く応じなかったことに落胆し、中間選挙で「彼らに票を入れるつもりはない」と打ち明けた。◇誘致の「象徴」住民の怒りは選挙情勢に表れている。上院選では、副大統領に就くため上院議員を辞めたバンス氏の後任である共和党現職ジョン・ヒューステッド氏が民主党元職シェロッド・ブラウン氏に対し、やや劣勢のもようだ。ブラウン氏はオハイオにデータセンターが多いのは、ヒューステッド氏が副知事時代に税制優遇を通じて誘致したからだと主張。同氏こそ「データセンターの『象徴』」だと批判する選挙広告を展開する。知事選は、24年大統領選で共和党の候補者指名争いに挑戦したビベク・ラマスワミ氏と民主党のエイミー・アクトン氏による新人同士の対決。こちらも共和党の劣勢が伝えられている。オハイオなどの「ラストベルト（さび付いた工業地帯）」は16年大統領選でトランプ氏支持に流れ、当選に大きく貢献したとされる。そうした地域での苦戦に共和党は危機感を募らせ、トランプ、バンス両氏とも選挙戦終盤にオハイオ入りを繰り返している。それでもデータセンター推進の姿勢は崩していない。トランプ氏は今月3日の集会で、データセンターにより「オハイオに大きな収益が見込める。追い出すわけにいかない」と訴えた。バンス氏は9日、データセンターを「経済の原動力にする」と強調した。国内政治に詳しいシンシナティ大のデービッド・ニーベン教授は、共和党がオハイオの上院選や知事選で敗れれば「恥ずかしい事態だ」と指摘。バンス氏がトランプ氏の後継大統領を目指す上で「決してプラスにならない」との見方を示した。（ピクア＝米オハイオ州＝時事）。

title: フランス各地 デモ乗じ破壊や略奪
body:
【パリ＝上地洋実】フランスで１７日、物価高への対策などを求める全国規模のデモが行われ、内務省によると全国で５５万人が参加した。これまで教育環境の改善を求めてきた高校生たちも加わり、近年では最大規模のデモになった。デモに乗じた破壊行為や店舗での略奪行為が横行し、各地で大きな混乱が生じた。【写真】放火され激しく燃え上がる仏中部リモージュの市庁舎（１７日）
デモはＳＮＳ上での呼びかけが契機となり、内務省によると、国内１１０か所で行われた。労働組合や環境団体などが加わり、物価高やエネルギー価格高騰への対策を政府に訴えた。また、９月から抗議活動を続けてきた高校生らも参加し、教員不足や校舎の老朽化に対する改善を求めた。
一方、一部の参加者が暴徒化し、治安部隊と衝突した。パリでは目抜き通りに面する店舗が襲撃され、路上に駐車された車が放火された。中部リモージュでは、市庁舎が放火されて大部分が焼失した。市庁舎は１８８３年に建てられた歴史的な建造物だった。南部マルセイユで市庁舎の扉が壊されたほか、南東部リヨンで観光案内所が燃やされた。
内務省によると、今回のデモでの拘束者数は２０００人に上り、警察官や消防隊員ら６００人が負傷した。ＡＦＰ通信によると、全国で１５００の小売店が襲撃を受け、被害額は数億ユーロと見込まれている。マクロン大統領は１７日、ＳＮＳに「破壊や襲撃、略奪に加わった者は、起訴され処罰される」と投稿し、厳しく取り締まる考えを示した。

title: 対露制裁見送り 米ウの亀裂深刻
body:
【キーウ共同】トランプ米大統領がロシア産軽油への制裁緩和や制裁法の実施見送りを決定したことにウクライナが猛反発し、両国関係の亀裂が深刻化している。ゼレンスキー大統領は17日「（米国の）制裁解除は続く」と述べ、トランプ氏への不信感をあらわにした。ウクライナ軍が使う米衛星通信網の軍事用サービスの利用制限も継続しているとした。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年
対ロ融和姿勢に傾くトランプ氏に対し、米議会からも「プーチン大統領に屈服した」との批判が噴出。11月の米中間選挙で与党共和党の劣勢が伝えられる中、トランプ氏は燃料価格の引き下げに躍起になっている。制裁法の実施見送りについて「米国と世界にとって良い決定」と反論した。制裁法は、7月に死去した共和党重鎮のグラム上院議員が主導した。侵攻を続けるロシアへの圧力を強められるはずだったが、ゼレンスキー氏はトランプ政権が「完全に無視」したとX（旧ツイッター）で不満を表明。制裁緩和は「プーチン氏に経済的な利得を与え、攻撃をさらに継続させるだけだ」と批判した。

title: 米与野党 対露制裁巡り批判が噴出
body:
【ワシントン共同】トランプ米大統領が16日夜、ウクライナ侵攻を続けるロシアへの制裁法実施見送りを表明したことを受け、米議会の与野党の議員から17日「ロシアのプーチン大統領に屈服した」などと激しい批判が噴出した。一方、トランプ氏は記者団に「米国と世界にとって良い決定」と反論した。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年
11月3日の中間選挙を控え、攻勢を強める野党民主党の上院トップ、シューマー院内総務は声明で「ロシア経済を延命させることで、トランプ氏の悪魔との取引はますます汚らわしいものとなった」と断じた。ベイヤー下院議員もX（旧ツイッター）で「トランプ氏がまたもプーチンに屈服し、ウクライナを再び裏切った」と非難した。普段はトランプ氏批判に慎重な与党共和党からも声が上がった。ティリス上院議員は「ロシアの独裁者に屈服しているのは到底容認できない」と指摘。コーニン上院議員も、法案を主導した共和党重鎮の故リンゼー・グラム上院議員の名前を挙げて「リンゼーはがくぜんとするだろう」と訴えた。制裁法は10月18日に導入される予定だった。

title: SUBARU 20年代後半にSDV投入へ
body: SUBARUは18日、ソフトウエアを更新して性能を向上させる次世代車「SDV」を2020年代後半に投入する方針を明らかにした。【写真特集】ジャパンモビリティショー2025SDVの前提となる新たな「電子制御ユニット（ECU）」を独自開発。ブレーキなどの車両制御と運転支援機能を一体でコントロールする。柴田英司常務執行役員は栃木県佐野市の同社施設で開いた開発戦略説明会で「超高機能なものではなく、便利に使ってもらえるようにしたい」と述べ、価格を抑えて普及を目指す考えを示した。新たなECUの核となる半導体は米アドバンスト・マイクロ・デバイシズ（AMD）と共同開発した。機能を最適化することで手頃な価格を実現する考えだ。また、車両開発にシミュレーションなどのデジタル技術を導入することなどにより、開発期間をこれまでより4割程度短縮する。

title: 長雨や日照不足の影響 農家苦悩
body:
長雨や日照不足が葉物野菜などに深刻な影響を与え、価格高騰が食卓を直撃している。農林水産省によると、レタスは平年に比べて2倍以上。白菜やキャベツも1.5倍以上と値上がりしている。今月中は下がる見込みはないという。【画像】長雨が影響？　どんどん伸びる雑草…対処法は「根っこから抜く」「花を見つけたら取り除く」「枯れるまで待つ」今もなお続く農家の苦悩を追跡取材した。
『news LOG』が、各地の農家から集めた野菜や畑の写真。腐ってしまったレタスや、カビが生える病気にかかったナスも。注目したのは、緑色に濁った水に覆われた畑の写真。いったいどんな被害にあったのか…。16日、茨城県八千代町。これから収穫の時期を迎えるはずだったキャベツ。その畑を見つめる人がいた。
この地域の農家を取りまとめる八千代組合の赤松弘貴代表。赤松さんが見せてくれた映像は、8月ごろから続く大雨で冠水した畑。
水が引かないまま約1か月、畑の広い範囲で藻が発生した。水につかったままのキャベツは病気になり、葉が黄色くなってしまっていた。
八千代組合 赤松弘貴代表「全体でいくと本当に50％、半分はやられている」約30の農家が所属する組合全体で、3000万円ほどの損失が出る見込みだという。
次に向かったのは白菜農家。ここ茨城県は白菜の生産量が日本一だ。案内してくれたのは、白菜の苗を植えたという畑…news LOG「結構ぬかるんでますね、まだ足元も」大木農園 大木実さん「もう真っ白でしょ？このようになっている」
news LOG「あーそっか、苗か」白く枯れてしまっているのは、植えたばかりだったという白菜の苗。相次ぐ大雨で畑は冠水し、苗は全滅。
今年はもう、白菜をつくることはできないという…。去年およそ2000万円だった白菜の売り上げは。大木農園 大木実さん「今年はゼロだよ、もうゼロ」
さらに、新たな場所で栽培を始めた人も。茨城県常総市の白菜農家、井上真晴さん。news LOG「今年の雨は異常だったんですね？」常総井上農園 井上真晴さん「異常ですね。誰も経験したことがない」去年10月、青々と順調に育っていた白菜だったが…。ことしは畑が冠水。白菜が育てられなくなったという。このため、隣の市にある別の畑を借り、そこで白菜を育てる決断をしたという。その畑を案内してもらった。しかし、そこに白菜があるようには見えない...そのワケは。

title: 東芝 難関大生から再評価される今
body: 2015年に発覚した不正会計問題などで経営危機に陥り、上場廃止となった「東芝」。ところがAI時代を迎え、難関大学の理系学生から改めて注目されている。なぜいま、東芝が選ばれているのか。【一覧】2026年度最新　主要国公立大学の「人気企業115社」就職者数はこちら＊　　＊　　＊かつて経営危機が報じられた「東芝」がいま、難関大生から再評価されている。就職支援サイト「ワンキャリア」に掲載されている口コミでは、東芝は「技術力を高められそう」「未来を創る安心・安全」「就職先としてかなり人気」と新卒学生から称賛されているのだ。東芝は2015年に不正会計が発覚し、23年に株式上場を廃止。経営の立て直しを進めるなかで26年度は東京大から8人が就職した。理系学生の人気企業ランキング（27年卒マイナビ・日経大学生就職企業人気ランキング）は、前年の89位から74位に上昇した。さらに夏季・冬季インターンシップの受け入れ人数は、ここ2年で倍増。23年度は約600人だったが、25年度は2倍の1200人を受け入れた。今年度はさらに増加見込みだという。とはいえ、不祥事のニュースを覚えている親から子どもが東芝に就職するのを心配されることはないのだろうか。「少なくとも私が担当する範囲では、親御さんから反対されたので説得するための材料がほしい、などの相談を内定者から受けたことはありません」と、採用センターの熊谷真由美さんは言う。■学生が説明会で「えっ」追い風の一つは、やはりAIだ。生成AIの普及により、データセンターのエネルギー需要に対応する送変電配電事業や、膨大なデータの保存を担うハードディスクドライブ（HDD）などの事業が好調だ。26年4～6月期の営業損益と売上高営業利益率（ROS）、当期純損益は過去最高、営業損益は前年同期比2.8倍の1119億円だった。だが、就活を始めたばかりの学生たちが抱く東芝のイメージは“今の姿”ではないという。熊谷さんは言う。「接点のある学生さんの半分くらいは、いまだに東芝を白物家電のメーカーだと思っています」いまも“東芝ブランド”の冷蔵庫や洗濯機は売られているが、家電事業はすでに中国の家電大手である美的集団に売却されている。「送変電配電、量子暗号通信などの事業を紹介すると、学生さんの反応が変わりますね。いま、東芝はBtoBの企業なのですと説明すると、『えっ』と驚くように顔を上げる学生さんもいます」（熊谷さん）

title: 東大も新設「デザイン学部」とは
body:
東京大学が2027年秋、新学部「カレッジ・オブ・デザイン」を開設する。近年ビジネスの現場でも「デザイン思考」という言葉が聞かれるようになったが、全国の大学でも「デザイン」を掲げる学部が増えている。就職にも強いと言われる「デザイン学部」だが、授業では何を学び、どんな力が身につくのか。【一覧】2026年度最新　主要国公立大学の「人気企業115社」就職者数はこちら＊　　＊　　＊東京大は2027年秋、新学部「College of Design（カレッジ・オブ・デザイン）」を開設する。実はいま、全国で「デザイン」を掲げる学部が続々と誕生している。ただ、ここでいうデザインは、絵を描いたり、商品の見た目を考えることを指すわけではない。一体、何を学ぶのか。全国に先駆けて、09年に「デザイン工学部」が創設された芝浦工業大の佐々木毅教授は言う。「本質は、問題を発見し、解決するところにあります」佐々木教授によれば、まず製品やサービスを使う人に、どんな困りごとがあるのかを探ったうえで、ひらめきだけに頼らず、データを分析する。そのうえで、情報、機械、電気などの技術を使って解決策を考える学問なのだという。それゆえ、一つの専門技術だけを磨くのではない。1年生で「デザイン思考」を学ぶ必修科目があり、数学や物理、工学、プログラミング、統計分析などを勉強する。学年が上がると、自身の専門性を軸に、リサイクルやヘルスケアなどの応用領域の知見を広げることも可能だ。こうして企業活動でも必要な「デザイン思考」を持った学生を育てるのだ。
■愛犬がカメラを見てくれないでは、一般の工学部とは何が違うのか。例えば、機械加工で、従来よりも精度を高める技術が実現できたとしても、「その技術を何に生かすのかという視点が欠けていれば、技術の進歩が新たな価値の創出につながるとは限りません。大切なのは、精度の向上そのものを目的とするのではなく、実現したい製品や解決したい課題を起点に、必要な精度や技術を考えることです。技術者は、精度を高めること自体が目的化し、その技術の応用先や社会的な意義を見失ってしまうことがあります」と佐々木教授は言う。もちろん、技術を深く追求することも大切だ。ただ、デザイン工学部では、技術を高めることだけを目的にしない。「本当の目的は何だったのか。その技術を使って、誰のどんな問題を解決するのか。そこを考え、実際に形にするトレーニングを積んでいます」身近な困りごとが、研究のタネになることもある。犬が大好きなある学生は、愛犬の写真を撮ろうとしても、なかなかカメラを見てくれないことに目を付けた。そこで、音声で犬をカメラ目線に誘導し、写真を撮りやすくするシステムを作った。他にも、パソコンが苦手な高齢者が遠隔でゲームを楽しめるように、盤上に透明のコマを置くと白や黒の色が付く「オセロ」を開発した学生もいた。カメラがコマを読み取って色を投影する「画像認識技術」を使ったという。佐々木教授の研究室では、大学院生を中心に学生たちは第1希望の企業への就職を果たしているという。27年卒はアクセンチュア、日立製作所、東京電力、スズキなどに内定した。同大によると、デザイン工学部では企画職や商品開発系の職を目指す学生も多い傾向にあるという。「いくら優秀なAIであっても、『何か役に立つものを考えてください』と聞かれただけでは、意味のある製品やサービスを提案することは難しいでしょう。やはり『そもそも何を作るべきか』『誰のどんな問題を解決するのか』といった具体的な課題や要求に落とし込むところには、人間の仕事が残ると考えています。何を設計するのかを学ぶことで、AIを使って新しい製品やサービスを生み出せる人材になることができると思います」（佐々木教授）

title: ガソリンスタンドで子が給油 危険
body:
ガソリンスタンドで給油を行う親子連れ、よく見ると幼い子どもがノズルを握っていて……。子どもに給油をさせる行為について「絶対にやめて」と注意喚起を行ったガソリンスタンド店員の投稿が、ネット上で話題を呼んでいる。給油に潜む危険とは、どのようなものがあるのか。投稿者の男性に詳しい話を聞いた。【動画】静電気から発生した火花が一瞬でガソリンに引火する様子「皆さん子供の時に親御さんの代わりに給油させたりもし、今給油させてる人います？　もし良かったらなぜさせてるのか教えて欲しいです」今月上旬、SNS上で話題を呼んだガソリンスタンドでの子どもの給油を巡る投稿。ガソリンスタンドのスタッフという投稿者は、未就学児や小学校低学年の子どもに給油をさせる親が多いことや、注意しても舌打ちや「横で見てるからいいだろ！」と逆ギレをされることについて、疑問の思いをつづっている。投稿は拡散。「子どもに給油させるなんて危険すぎる」「レジでもなんでも、子どもにやらせたがる親が不思議」など、さまざまな声が寄せられている。ガソリンスタンドで働く20代の投稿者は、子どもが給油ノズルを操作することの危険について、強く注意を促す。「大人が給油する様子を見て、子どもが真似したがるので、気にせずやらせている親が多いように感じます。ガソリンは揮発性が高く、静電気での引火・爆発の危険はもとより、体にかかるとやけどを負ったり、目に入ると失明したり、気化した可燃性のガスを吸い込んでしまう危険もある。車の給油口も子どもの顔と同じくらいの高さで、非常に危険です。絶対にやめてほしい」中には毎回注意しても舌打ちしたり、すごんでくる親もいるといい、今回、いら立ちと注意喚起の思いから、SNSでの投稿を決意したという。JAF（日本自動車連盟）の公式サイトも、「給油作業する際には、子どもが近づかないように注意しましょう」と注意喚起。「ガソリンは目に見えませんが給油中も気化しています。よって、火気厳禁は言うまでもありませんが、万が一、給油口から溢れてしまった場合には、一度に大量のガソリンが気化してしまうので、とくに注意が必要です。もし大量のガソリンが溢れてしまった場合は、セルフスタンドであっても店員が常駐していますので、店員にその旨を連絡しましょう」とガソリンの危険性を訴えている。「セルフのガソリンスタンドであっても、監視カメラがついており、こちらから強制的に給油を止められるボタンもあります。どうか危険な給油行為はやめてほしい」と投稿者。予期せぬ事故を防ぐためにも、ルールに則った使用が求められる。
ENCOUNT編集部／クロスメディアチーム

title: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France
summary: French President Emmanuel Macron gives a national address after widespread disorder and as some looting continued in Paris.
body:
Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of Paris
French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.
In a national address from the Élysée Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.
The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight
On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
A view of the damage inside Limoges town hall on Sunday morning
Speaking near the ruined building, Annèyse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody."
"It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Fires were lit and shops looted during smaller scale disorder in Paris on Sunday
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.
A man tries to extinguish a fire in Paris on Sunday
Student protests which began last month escalated significant on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.
The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised Nuñez and police chiefs on social media.
He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".
Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

title: 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight
summary: A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests
body:
A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests on Saturday.
Dramatic footage shared online shows the 19th-century building engulfed in flames, with the spire of its clock tower later collapsing.
On Sunday, stunned residents watched as firefighters, who had battled the blaze through the night, assessed the building's structural integrity. Officials have not yet confirmed whether the town hall is at risk of collapse.
"Damaging heritage buildings because you're angry with the government is selfish", one resident told the BBC.
BBC correspondent Chris Bockman reports from Limoges.

title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
summary: Prime Minister Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".
body:
Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.
Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".
The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity".
"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.
The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.
Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.
Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.
Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.
"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.
A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.
"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he  said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."
Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.
News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.
Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".
The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.
In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".
What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base
Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.
Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.
The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down.
Wainwright is about 200km (125 miles) from Edmonton, the provincial capital
The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units.
"It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province.
STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed.
Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance.
Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said.
"I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie".
Additional reporting by Lisa Lambert

title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
body:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.
"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".
Trumpblocked numerous sanctions on Russiaon Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.
In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".
Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.
Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.
In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".
Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday
Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.
The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.
Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.
However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.
Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.

title: Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US
summary: The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from Chicago, where communities are battling a new wave of synthetic drugs.
body:

A new wave of synthetic drugs is sweeping across the United States, raising fear of a worsening drug crisis.
Earlier this year, President Donald Trump pledged a crackdown on drug cartels, proscribing many as terrorist organisations.
Drug overdose deaths have fallen from a peak of around 110,000 in 2022, down to roughly 70,000 last year.
However, America's decades-long drug crisis may be accelerating and authorities are increasingly concerned about cheaper, more powerful synthetic drugs, including an animal tranquilliser called tranq.

title: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
summary: Tech firm Nscale says it is still committed to building the site in Essex.
body:
Nscale said it remained committed to building a £2bn AI data centre in Loughton
A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project.
Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open apioneering facility in Loughton, Essex.
However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement.
A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment.
"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said.
"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term."
What is the new AI supercomputer planned for Essex?
The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year.
But as firstreported by the Telegraph on Sunday,external, Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s.
"This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC.
Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States.
The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens.
Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer.

title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
summary: More property asking prices are being cut than at any time in 15 years, data shared with the BBC shows.
body:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.
The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.
The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.
Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.
"Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove.
"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."
Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly £21,000 cut from a typically valued home.
Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price.
The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023.
Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed.
Withmortgage rates at a three-year high, Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable.
So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed.
September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year.
Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price.
The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell.
Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Rightmove.
'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak?
You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it
Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, andextra problems for those selling leasehold propertiesin England.
One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier."
Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home".
But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget.
Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial.
"That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said.
Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price.
"The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said.
But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it.
In Scotland, theHome Report system,externalrequires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market.
Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain.
His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London.
He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England.

title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
summary: Trading standards officers say AI is "super-charging" existing scams through clones and fake websites.
body:
Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.
Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.
If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say.
AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.
For the first time, it has drawn up anAI scam watchlist,externalhighlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.
Cloned or new websites that look polished and professional in rapid time and at a low cost
Romance scams in which AI is used to remember victims' personal details and keep conversations going over weeks or months
AI-generated deepfake videos and voice-cloned audio is used to impersonate family members or close friends asking for money in an "emergency"
Error-free, personalised phishing emails, text messages and social media posts can be generated by AI on a huge scale
Some of the old scam-avoidance techniques may now be less successful due to the benefits of AI.
Typos or grammatical errors can no longer be relied on to spot scams, says consumer group Which?.
Some of the ways to protect yourself, according to trading standards, include:
Never sending money, gift cards or personal or financial information to someone you have not met in person
Doing your research - such as checking whether a shop's address is real, using theFinancial Conduct Authority's Firm Checker,external, to ensure a company is authorised to give financial advice, and contacting a business directly to check whether a job advert is real
Not assuming someone is genuine just because you've heard their voice or seen them on a video call
In general, they say stop and think before paying, sharing personal information or taking action. You should be especially wary of pressure or urgency because criminals want you to act before you have time to think.
Fraud and scams can be reported toReport Fraud,externalor by calling on 0300 1232040, or you can call the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline on 0808 223 1133 for advice.

title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.
body:
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.
There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine
Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?
summary: The sports industry's lucrative business model is being undermined by dodgy TV sticks and illegal streaming links, writes Theo Leggett.
body:
"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than £20m on new players.
The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of £8.5m.
That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when £100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.
All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than £300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.
It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.
But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.
This year's Champions League final - won by Paris Saint-Germain - sparked an argument about TV viewing rights
And this summer saw signs of a clampdown.
In August, a man in Lancashire was jailed for six and a half years for running an illegal streaming service that police said had generated almost £1m in illicit profits. In June, a postman from Pembrokeshire was jailed for over three years for selling illegal subscriptions and supplying pirate software to nearly 2,000 people.
A third man, from Merseyside, received a suspended 32-month sentence in August for similar offences. Several pubs have been fined thousands of pounds for screening matches illegally.
TV companies that have paid huge sums for exclusive rights to high-profile sports are having to work harder than ever to protect their investments. To some extent, broadcasters used to see copyright theft as a cost of doing business: irritating and expensive, but not an existential threat. But now, as advertising revenues fall, and viewers move away from long-term subscription services like Sky or TNT Sports, the industry is getting seriously worried.
There is a great deal at stake. The Premier League alone is a sporting monster. In its most recent deal, it sold its viewing rights to domestic audiences for £6.7bn over four years, with almost as much coming from foreign rights. Armed with bundles of TV cash, clubs have been able to attract the finest players in the world. That in turn has given the league a major international profile.
Although football has been the main beneficiary of paid-for TV in the UK, other competitions such as Formula One, Six Nations rugby and the Wimbledon tennis championships have also commanded very high fees for selling exclusive rights. Live sport on free-to-air television has become increasingly rare.
Yet that wealth could be threatened by a surge in piracy and illegal viewing. The practice is most common among younger, digital-native audiences, who each year become a larger and larger share of sports fans. But many older viewers also seem comfortable with it.
Rupert Murdoch (left) launched Sky TV with the broadcaster Andrew Neil in 1989. It went on to transform Britain's sports-watching landscape
"For 18 to 34-year-olds, it's over 70% who admit to doing this regularly," says Daniel Monaghan, a researcher at Ampere Analysis. "Over half of 35 to 44s admit to doing it, and about a third of those aged 45 to 64."
This year's Champions League final went behind a paywall in the UK for the first time in more than 30 years. Viewers were asked to pay at least £4.99 to watch it, prompting a backlash, including from the then-prime minister, Arsenal fan Sir Keir Starmer.
"Hardworking people shouldn't have to fork out for a subscription to watch this match," he wrote on X.
Many simply refused to pay: 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match in the UK, according to research carried out by the Gaming Compliance International consultancy, on behalf of the Guardian newspaper. That compared to around seven million people who watched it legally in the UK.
One prolific user of pirate streams is "Kiran", a tech sector worker in his 30s, who prefers not to give his real name. A keen Arsenal fan, he likes to watch Premier League and Champions League games, as well as big matches in Spain's La Liga. He has a paid subscription to TNT Sports, but uses streaming websites to see games that are not available there.
Many fans watched this year's Champions League final legally at pubs - but at home, 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match, according to one analysis
"What it comes down to is the financial side - that's the big one - and ease of access as well," he says. "Getting every single game will cost you hundreds of pounds a year."
Meanwhile the streams he uses are free, with links readily obtainable on social media.
But there's another issue, he says: the famous blackout. Games taking place between 14:45 and 17:15 on a Saturday are not usually screened live in the UK, a decades-old policy designed to protect crowds at lower league matches. But broadcasters outside the UK can and do show those matches, fuelling pirated streams.
"I pretty much got into streaming stuff due to [the blackout]," Kiran says, "and I'd say I sort of did it a bit more as subscriptions got more expensive."
Those searching for pirated material have plenty of options. Streaming links, along with advice on how to avoid their pitfalls, are freely available in online discussion groups. These links, used by Kiran and his friends, have practical downsides – such as frequent buffering or poor quality, or platforms that disappear without warning. In some cases, they can also be used to bombard viewers with explicit ads for porn sites.
Many people prefer to access illegal content with a streaming device, such as an Amazon Fire Stick, a pocket-sized gadget that plugs into a TV. The sticks are legitimate products, but they can also be "sideloaded" with unauthorised software, allowing pirates to mimic the output of legitimate outlets by offering packages of selected channels.
A third option for illicit viewing is to use a virtual private network, or VPN, which effectively allows your computer to pretend it's in a different country, one in which access to sports programming is cheaper than it is in the UK (or totally free).
Earlier this year, the Sports Industry Group found that 58% of fans surveyed considered illegal streaming to be socially acceptable.
Stan Collymore's transfer from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool, for £8.5m, set a British record in 1995
That may be because viewers have simply come to resent the amount of money they are expected to pay.
As the government's Intellectual Property Office puts it, "a main driver of illegal content access is the perception of unfair or high pricing for legal services".
A British person wanting to access all live Premier League games, for example, would need subscriptions to both Sky Sports and TNT Sports. Throw in some matches from Spain, or European Champions Cup rugby, and Premier Sports has to be added to the list. Many boxing matches and NFL games are on DAZN. A keen fan could easily end up paying £80 to £100 a month.
Until relatively recently, clamping down on piracy was not seen as a priority by the broadcasters themselves. They were focused on audience growth, and copyright infringement was simply a cost of doing business.
Formula 1 is another sport that's been able to command high fees for selling exclusive TV viewing rights
In some parts of the industry, it was even seen as a benefit. In 2013, the then-chief executive of Time Warner, Jeff Bewkes, notoriously welcomed the drama series Game of Thrones becoming the most pirated show in the world. He suggested that the attention generated by illegal viewing was "better than an Emmy" because it helped create buzz and ultimately attract new subscribers.
Now, however, the mood has shifted. Conventional broadcasting is under pressure as advertising revenues fall and viewers move away from long-term subscription services, towards more flexible offers from streaming platforms such as Netflix, Amazon Prime and Apple TV. Both Sky and TNT Sports have reported losses.
According to a recent report by WPI Economics, illegal sports streaming costs the broadcasting industry about £700m each year.
And piracy is already having impacts on the pitch.
At a conference last year, Tom Burrows, the head of global rights at the sports streaming platform DAZN, described piracy as a "huge problem" for his company, and "almost a crisis for the sports rights industry".
Just months after he made those comments, DAZN agreed to end its deal with the French football league, under which it was allowed to screen the top tier of French football matches within France. The agreement followed a bitter dispute, which focused in part on the streamer's claims the league had not done enough to combat piracy – although subscriber numbers were also understood to be an issue.
Even though DAZN paid a reported €100m (£85m) to end the contract (along with outstanding rights fees worth another €140m), its departure created a hole in the French league's finances. It was left to set up its own streaming service, and the amount of broadcast income fell from roughly €700m per year to €412m this season, according to figures compiled by football-finance.com.
For a European powerhouse like Paris St Germain, with plenty of other revenue sources, this probably matters little. But for smaller teams it has been a serious problem. title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
summary: The Green Party leader said, while he wanted to amend it, the motion would stand until 2028.
body:
Watch: Polanski says practical application of Zionism is racist
Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.
The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.
The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It divided the party andsparked a major backlashfrom MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.
The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, andthreatened his leadership.
He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.
The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.
Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.
"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."
He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".
Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."
Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner.
"I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel.
"One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."
Polanski had previously said he wouldnot have voted for the motionwithout two amendments.
The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.
Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.
Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.
Asked if he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said he did not think this was controversial, adding: "I think what's controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years."
Kuenssberg asked Polanski if he accepted that for many Jewish people, Zionism was the right to have a safe place to live, or homeland.
"I think that's what people think it means, but actually in practical application - which is what we're talking about here - that homeland has come to the cost of the Palestinian people," Polanski, who is Jewish, said.
"I want equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - the practical application of Zionism has not resulted in that."
When questioned if he thought Israel had a right to exist, he said he did not think "any state has a right to exist under international law".
And asked if he would apologise for his handling of the row, as theJewish Greens chairVivien Lichtenstein has asked him to do, Polanski said: "I'm not sorry at all."
In response, Phil Rosenberg, president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, accused Polanski of being "all over the place" on the issue.
"Let us remember that, as of now, the Green Party's platform erases Jewish identity and experience, calls for Israel's elimination, and tells the vast majority of Jews, who overwhelmingly believe in the right of Israel to exist, that they are not welcome in the party," Rosenberg added.
Polanski has said no Jewish Green members will be excluded based on their faith or background - and that being Jewish and supporting Israel are "two separate things".
His latest comments come after afortnight of criticismfrom across the political spectrum over the motion.
Labour has said it willend power-sharing agreementswith the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it "antisemitic".Polanski said it was up to Green councillors to do what they saw fit.

title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
summary: Yvette Cooper also announces £140m investment in England's urgent care system, ahead of winter.
body:
No patient should be treated in a corridor, Yvette Cooper says
The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.
Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.
She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.
The health secretary has announced £140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.
The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.
Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.
The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.
"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.
Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."
The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.
Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.
According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.
On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.
Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.
"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.
Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.
Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."
Two-year-old Finlay Roberts died after spending hours in a crowded hospital corridor
The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened extended their condolences to the family.
They said they continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.
"Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions," they said.
On Friday health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), also expressed their concern over corridor care, writing a letter to the health secretary urging her to take action.
It said the practice was fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it.
This weekend Cooper announced £140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.
The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.
Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from.
It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.
Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.
NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying earlier this month there were"ominous" signs of winter pressurealready affecting hospitals.
Swords said there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year.
RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point".
"The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.
Correction 18 October 2026: This article and this note have been updated after earlier versions incorrectly stated the location of Finlay Roberts' death.

title: Ex-top official Robbins reaches settlement with government over sacking
summary: Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson.
body:
Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top official in the Foreign Office in April
Sir Olly Robbins has reached an out-of-court settlement with the government, after he was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson to be US ambassador.
Sir Olly was fired by then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer earlier this year, after it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.
The FDA union, which represented him in the legal action, said Sir Olly had been made a "scapegoat" to "mask the misjudgement" of Sir Keir.
How much Sir Olly received in the settlement has not been made public.
It came after he requested a judicial review over the decision to dismiss him.
A government spokesperson said Sir Olly "had a distinguished public service career over three decades".
A statement added: "The government has reached a settlement with Sir Oliver following his dismissal. We will not be commenting further on HR matters."
Lord Mandelson was announced as the UK's ambassador to the US in December 2024, before in-depth vetting had been carried out, and formally took up the role in February 2025 after being granted security clearance.
Just seven months later, he was sacked after further information emerged about his previous friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Sir Olly was sacked in April, in the wake of a Guardian story that revealed the peer's security clearance had been granted despite vetting officials raising concerns, with the prime minister later saying he was "furious" he had not been informed at the time.
Sir Keir has previously said he sacked Sir Olly after not accepting his explanation for why clearance was granted, telling MPs in April: "I did ask him, and I did not accept his explanation. That is why I sacked him."
Sir Olly has since defended his role in the process, saying that the government's vetting processes must "remain absolutely confidential".
He previously told MPs that he had not seen the documentation from UK Security Vetting, the government's in-house vetting unit, containing their vetting assessment of Lord Mandelson.
He said that instead, he was given an oral briefing, during which he was told the vetting agency considered Mandelson to be a "borderline case", but that the Foreign Office may wish to grant clearance with "appropriate risk management".
Starmer sacks top Foreign Office official after Mandelson vetting revelations
Key evidence from sacked official at heart of Mandelson vetting row
Dave Penman, head of the FDA union, said: "This settlement may bring an end to the Judicial Review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.
"The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgement of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations - which is quite the feat.
"We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process."
Sir Olly said: "I am grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time.
"I want to thank the FDA for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life".
Sir Olly, who was appointed to the Foreign Office job in early 2025, has held a number of senior civil service roles and was previously the government's lead official during Brexit negotiations with the EU.

title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
summary: On his first substantive trip to Scotland since becoming PM, he says politicians should focus on solutions "right now" and move beyond the issue of Scottish independence.
body:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).
Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.
SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since theSmith Commission report was publishedin 2014.
The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.
He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".
Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
However, he described Scotland as the most devolved nation in the UK but "one of the most centralised in Europe".
"During my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland's regions and cities," he said.
"Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.
"This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people."
Burnham to visit Scotland during SNP conference
Burnham - Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas decisions coming 'shortly'
The Scottish government set out plans for a radical rethink of the country's regional authorities last month.
A new two-tiered system would see the32 local authorities replaced with six new regional authorities.
They would have power over major issues such as economic growth and education.
Below that, between 120 and 160 community authorities would govern more local issues, such as licensing and town centre improvements.
It would be the most significant change to Scotland's regional makeup since the current system was introduced by the UK government in 1996.
Burnham acknowledged that the Scottish government was working on local government reform, but said this had to "move faster".
It is not clear exactly what powers might be exercised at regional level other than employment support.
Burnham appears to expect the Scottish government to devolve some of its own powers to regional authorities.
But he made clear that he will not impose a model of regional devolution like the metropolitan mayors that already operate in England.
Instead he wants to try and agree a way forward with further discussions when the prime minister sits down with all the devolved first ministers at the end of this month.
John Swinney denied that too much power was centralised at Holyrood
Burnham also called for an end to "tribal politics" between the Scottish and UK governments.
He said he and Swinney "agreed on some things" but "didn't have to agree on everything".
Swinney is expected to promote his renewed push for independence in his keynote speech at the SNP conference on Saturday.
He previously welcomed Burnham telling MPs thata border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Irelandif there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.
But Burnham later pushed back on that by telling Swinney at a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".
Asked whether devolving power more locally in Scotland would make independence more or less likely, the prime minister said: "I don't want to be the last PM of the UK.
"I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.
"In my view, people in Scotland are suffering from the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else, and I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people right now."
He added: "Too much time is wasted on those dramas, it consumes too much energy."
Stephen Flynn - who was the SNP's leader at Westminster before becoming the Transport Secretary at Holyrood - said the Scottish government would welcome the opportunity to be handed more power over the country's economic prospects.
He said: "Interestingly the first minister sent a letter to the prime minister on Monday where he outlined a number of points he would like to see engagement on.
"This was number seven on that list, so we will of course engage with the prime minister fully in respect of his announcement today."
Before Burnham's speech, First Minister John Swinney said he was interested in "working constructively" with Westminster, adding he was "all for the Scottish Parliament having as many powers" as possible.
UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham should be focusing on creating new opportunities in the energy sector.
She said: "This regional devolution plan is more jobs for the boys. What Andy Burnham should be doing is granting new oil and gas licences in the north sea."
"Devolution is a process, not a solution."

title: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
summary: Downing Street says Sarah Helm, the wife of Jonathan Powell, "does not represent the government in any capacity".
body:
Jonathan Powell is the government's national security adviser
Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office.
Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."
She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment.
On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action.
"It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required."
Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post.
The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking".
"Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said.
However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery."
He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian".
Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent.
Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics".
Earlier this year, four of the group's activistswere jailedafter causing £1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.
In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk.
The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group.
Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month.
Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland.
In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister.
